newsitem.title: GERMANY: German police brace for more anti-nuclear protests.
newsitem.headline: German police brace for more anti-nuclear protests.

text.p: Thousands of German police braced on Wednesday to protect a shipment of spent nuclear fuel from thousands of anti-nuclear activists determined to prevent it reaching a northern dump.

Police said they intended to move around 4,000 sit-down protesters who gatherered around the loading station at Dannenberg where the shipment arrived on Tuesday, and said they would use water cannons if necessary to shift the group.

On Tuesday hundreds of masked militants lobbed fire bombs and pelted police with stones to protest against the shipment, which is due to be moved by road to the Gorleben medium-term storage depot, east of Hanover, on Wednesday.
Two police officers were injured in the clashes and a thick cordon of police encircled about 250 demonstrators to take their fingerprints and personal details.

Police said it was not yet clear which route the trucks would take for the final 20-km (14-mile) stretch of the journey to Gorleben, because protesters had burrowed underneath roads and damaged the surface of others.
Protesters had also set up barricades. Police said repair work to some of the roads might be necessary.

The government defended its nuclear energy policies, conservatives slammed the activists for "abusing the freedom to demonstrate" but the environmental Greens party defended the protests as an expression of popular dissent.

In Germany's biggest post-war security operation, some 30,000 police and border troops lined tracks along the train's route northwards on Monday to rein in thousands of activists who had defied the authorities' ban on demonstrating.
But the operation, costing an estimated 66 million marks ($39 million), seemed far from over as police faced the prospect of further disruption from 8,000 activists camped at Gorleben.
The shipment from two German power stations and a French reprocessing plant arrived eight hours late on Tuesday after a 20-hour journey disrupted by several protests en route.
